text: region crosses antimeridian best requested explicitly. example, Aleutian arc spans longitudes east west 180 degrees. data use continuous longitudes around 180 degrees, set antimeridian = TRUE geom_bathy(). x axis remains readable, labels expressed east west longitudes.
code: aleutians <- get_noaa(   lon = c(165, -145),   lat = c(50, 65),   resolution = 5,   antimeridian = TRUE ) aleutians |>   ggplot() +   geom_bathy(     aes(lon, lat, fill = depth),     antimeridian = TRUE,     expand = FALSE,     x_breaks = seq(165, 215, by = 10)   ) +   geom_coastline(linewidth = 0.4) +   geom_contour(     aes(lon, lat, z = depth),     breaks = seq(0, -7000, by = -500),     colour = "grey20",     linewidth = 0.15   ) +   scale_fill_bathy(     palette_ocean = "ocean_blues",     palette_land = "land_earth"   ) +   theme_bw()

title: Download bathymetry from the GEBCO download service — get_gebco
text: get_gebco uses workflow implemented official GEBCO Grid Subsetting App https://download.gebco.net/. function submits small JSON basket /api/queue, polls /api/queue/status/{basketId} basket ready, downloads resulting zip archive /api/queue/download/{basketId}, extracts NetCDF file, reads lat, lon, elevation variables, converts requested output class. current global GEBCO grids served GEBCO download service native resolution 15 arc-seconds, .e. 0.25 arc-minutes 0.0041667 decimal degrees. corresponds approximately 463 m equator. get_gebco() always returns native GEBCO resolution. Use reduce_bathy_resolution afterwards reduce spatial resolution locally without sending new request GEBCO. GEBCO also exposes higher-resolution regional experimental products download service, example polar grids beta multi-resolution layers. function intentionally targets default global longitude/latitude bathymetry layer whose NetCDF variables named lon, lat, elevation. GEBCO download service expects left <= right; areas crossing antimeridian therefore downloaded two geographic subsets, one eastern longitude bound 180 degrees one -180 degrees western longitude bound. two subsets stitched single bathy object whose longitudes expressed 0-360 degree range. get_noaa, order lon1/lon2 lat1/lat2 matter: function sorts coordinate bounds internally submitting requests GEBCO.

title: Download bathymetry from NOAA ETOPO 2022 — get_noaa
text: get_noaa() queries ETOPO 2022 database hosted NOAA, using coordinates area interest desired resolution. function uses NOAA ArcGIS image service exposed ImageServer backend NOAA Grid Extract tool, returns long tibble default, matrix class bathy class = "bathy". resolution argument expressed arc-minutes. function uses 15 arc-second ETOPO 2022 layer resolution = 0.25, 30 arc-second layer resolution = 0.5, 60 arc-second layer coarser resolutions. Values lower 0.5 rounded 0.25; values 0.5 1 rounded 0.5. Users can optionally write downloaded data disk keep = TRUE. identical query performed later, using longitudes, latitudes, resolution, antimeridian setting, get_noaa() load local file instead querying NOAA server . behaviour used preferentially reduce unnecessary queries NOAA service reduce data loading time. several identical queries forced download fresh data, cached csv file must renamed, removed, moved outside path. get_noaa() can download bathymetric data around antimeridian antimeridian = TRUE. antimeridian 180th meridian, located Pacific Ocean, east New Zealand Fiji west Hawaii Tonga. pair longitude values -150 150, two different areas can requested: 60 degree-wide area centered antimeridian antimeridian = TRUE, 300 degree-wide area centered prime meridian antimeridian = FALSE. Data around antimeridian require two distinct NOAA queries, keep = TRUE can especially useful case. Internally, get_noaa() downloads temporary GeoTIFF subsets using official ETOPO 2022 layer names used NOAA Grid Extract tool. temporary files written R's temporary directory removed soon converted bathy/tibble data. order longitude latitude bounds matter: get_noaa() sorts coordinate bounds internally querying NOAA. Longitude latitude bounds preferably supplied vector syntax lon = c(lon1, lon2) lat = c(lat1, lat2). explicit lon1, lon2, lat1, lat2 arguments remain available compatibility older code.
